n: After defeating Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon becomes master of the region. Jehoiakim submits for three years, then foolishly rebels.

f.g: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon about 605–562 BC.
Became his vassal, paying yearly tribute.

n: The Lord allows raiding bands from Babylon and Judah’s neighbors to attack Judah, fulfilling the prophets’ warnings. Scripture sees God’s hand behind the movements of nations.

f.g: Chaldeans—the people of southern Mesopotamia who ruled the Babylonian empire.

n: The narrator explains that this disaster is God’s judgment for the sins of Manasseh, whose evil had poisoned the nation for generations.
Especially unforgivable was the innocent blood Manasseh shed throughout Jerusalem—violence the people never truly repented of.

f.w: which the LORD would not pardon

n: The standard closing note for Jehoiakim points to the royal annals.

f.w: the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim

n: Jehoiakim dies around 598 BC, and his son Jehoiachin inherits a kingdom under siege. Jeremiah had prophesied a dishonorable end for Jehoiakim.

f.g: Also called Jeconiah or Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24; 1 Chronicles 3:16).

n: Egypt can no longer help Judah: Babylon now controls everything from the border of Egypt to the Euphrates. Judah’s hope in Egypt was misplaced.

f.g: Probably the Wadi el-Arish, a seasonal stream marking the border between Canaan and Egypt.

n: Jehoiachin becomes king at eighteen and reigns only three months before Babylon arrives.

f.g: The queen mother, who is named again in the surrender (verse 12).

n: Like his father, Jehoiachin does evil in the Lord’s sight.

f.w: according to all that his father had done

n: Babylon’s army surrounds Jerusalem in 597 BC to punish Jehoiakim’s rebellion.

f.g: Surrounded by an army to cut off supplies and force surrender.

n: Nebuchadnezzar himself comes to oversee the siege.

f.g: His officers were already conducting the siege when the king arrived.

n: Jehoiachin surrenders with his mother and court. Babylonian records also note this capture, dating it to about March 597 BC.

f.w: the eighth year of his reign
went out to the king of Babylon

n: Babylon strips the temple and palace treasures, exactly as Isaiah had told Hezekiah a century earlier. God’s word through His prophets proves true.

Ten thousand leading citizens, warriors and skilled workers are deported, leaving only the poorest. Removing leaders and craftsmen kept a conquered land weak. The prophet Ezekiel was among this group.

f.g: Skilled workers, especially metalworkers who could make weapons.

n: The king, his mother, his wives, his officials and the nation’s leaders are all taken to Babylon.
The total includes seven thousand soldiers and a thousand craftsmen—everyone fit for war. Babylon wanted to make sure Judah could not rebel again.
Nebuchadnezzar makes Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah king and renames him Zedekiah, showing he is Babylon’s appointee. Lehi’s ministry and departure began in Zedekiah’s first year.

f.g: Jehoiachin’s uncle; Mattaniah was another son of Josiah.

n: Zedekiah becomes king at twenty-one and reigns eleven years (about 597–586 BC). He is a full brother of Jehoahaz, sharing the same mother.
Zedekiah continues in evil. Jeremiah tells us he was a weak king who often consulted the prophet but lacked the courage to obey him.
Zedekiah eventually rebels against Babylon, which the narrator sees as part of God’s judgment unfolding. Prophets like Jeremiah—and Lehi—warned of destruction, but leaders refused to listen.

f.w: Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon
